subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of irritability in a gene positive adult with a hyperkinetic movement disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a neuropsychiatry clinic. A 45-year-old man attends with his wife. His father died at 58 with Huntington disease and he had predictive genetic testing 4 years ago that returned a CAG repeat length of 43.

His wife reports that over the past 9 months he has become quick-tempered, shouts at her over small frustrations, and once punched a door. He has stopped organising the family finances and now sits for long periods unless prompted, which she finds harder to manage than the temper.

He says he is not sad and denies losing pleasure in things, though he sleeps poorly and wakes early. He has no suicidal thoughts. On examination he has intermittent fidgety movements of the fingers and shoulders and an impersistent tongue protrusion. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 27 out of 30 with a low verbal fluency subscore. There are no hallucinations and no delusions. His wife asks whether anything can be done about the temper.

data_table.Examination: Intermittent fidgety finger and shoulder movements, impersistent tongue protrusion, no rigidity
data_table.Mental state: Irritable, reduced initiation, denies sadness or anhedonia, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 27 out of 30 with reduced verbal fluency
data_table.Genetics: CAG repeat length 43 on predictive testing 4 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management of his irritability?

options.text: Diazepam as required for episodes of agitation, with review of the frequency at 6 weeks
options.rationale: As-required benzodiazepines add sedation and fall risk to a progressive neurodegenerative illness and provide no sustained benefit for a symptom that is present most of the day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Sodium valproate titrated over 4 weeks, with a level and liver function checked afterwards
options.rationale: Valproate is used for irritability where mood instability is prominent or an antidepressant has failed, but it is not the first agent and adds sedation, weight gain and hepatic monitoring burden. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.text: Olanzapine at a low nightly dose, with weight and metabolic monitoring from the outset
options.rationale: An antipsychotic is the next step if a serotonergic agent fails, and it has the advantage of also suppressing chorea, but it carries metabolic and extrapyramidal burden and his movements are not yet disabling. The distinguishing consideration is whether chorea needs treating at the same time. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

options.text: Sertraline titrated over 4 weeks, with review of irritability and initiation at 6 weeks
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line for irritability and apathy in Huntington disease and are effective even when the patient does not describe sadness, since irritability in this illness is a frontostriatal symptom rather than a marker of depression. Starting here also avoids the metabolic and movement burden that an antipsychotic would add. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Tetrabenazine titrated over 4 weeks, with depression and suicidality screened at each visit
options.rationale: Tetrabenazine is licensed for chorea, not for irritability, and it depletes presynaptic monoamines, which causes or worsens depression and carries a recognised association with suicidality in a population whose suicide rate is already several times that of the general population. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disorder in which the psychiatric and cognitive features frequently precede the movement disorder by years and cause more day-to-day disability than the chorea itself. Irritability, apathy, depression and obsessionality are the commonest neuropsychiatric features, and apathy in particular is often mistaken by families for laziness or by clinicians for depression. Treatment of irritability begins with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, with an antipsychotic or valproate added or substituted when that fails, and the choice is influenced by whether chorea also needs suppression. Suicide risk is substantially elevated across the illness, peaking around the time of diagnosis and again when independence is lost, so it is asked about at every review. Care is multidisciplinary and includes genetic counselling for at-risk relatives, since predictive testing has implications for the whole family.
key_points: Psychiatric and cognitive symptoms often precede chorea and cause more functional impairment than the movements
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first line for irritability and apathy, regardless of whether sadness is reported
Antipsychotics treat both irritability and chorea but add metabolic and extrapyramidal burden
Tetrabenazine treats chorea but depletes monoamines and is associated with depression and suicidality
Suicide risk is elevated throughout, peaking at diagnosis and at loss of independence
explanation.pearls: A CAG repeat length of 40 or more is fully penetrant, 36 to 39 is reduced penetrance and 27 to 35 is an intermediate allele that does not cause disease but can expand on paternal transmission.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for Huntington disease

subtopic_detail: Excessive daytime sleepiness with laughter induced weakness in an adolescent treated for depression
stem:
A 17-year-old girl is referred to your adolescent psychiatry clinic because her depression has not responded to treatment. Twelve months ago her general practitioner diagnosed depression after her marks fell and she began falling asleep in class, and sertraline was started 6 months ago and titrated to a standard dose.

She tells you she still sees her friends every weekend, still enjoys her art and her part-time job, and describes her mood as fine apart from being embarrassed about school. Her appetite is unchanged and she denies early morning waking, guilt or hopelessness.

She sleeps from 10 pm to 7 am without difficulty getting off to sleep, then naps for an hour after school and wakes from those naps feeling refreshed for a few hours. Her mother adds that twice in the past year the girl's knees buckled and she sank to the ground while laughing hard with friends, staying fully aware throughout. Her Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 18 out of 24, her body mass index is 23, and her iron studies and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Mental state: Reactive affect, retained interest and enjoyment, no guilt or hopelessness, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Sleep history: Sleeps 10 pm to 7 am without initiation difficulty, refreshing afternoon naps, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 18 out of 24, two episodes of knee buckling during laughter with preserved awareness
data_table.Investigations: Iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits, body mass index 23

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline to the maximum tolerated dose and review her again in 4 weeks
options.rationale: She retains interest, enjoyment and reactivity with no guilt or hopelessness, so the diagnosis rather than the dose is the problem; increasing it prolongs a 12-month diagnostic delay. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance

options.text: Arrange polysomnography followed the next day by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Sleepiness with refreshing naps and episodes of laughter-triggered weakness with preserved awareness describes cataplexy, and the diagnosis of narcolepsy requires overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes of sleep disruption followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day. That sequence must be performed in the correct order, since a daytime test alone cannot be interpreted without knowing the preceding night's sleep. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance
Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Switch her from sertraline to venlafaxine and review her response in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Venlafaxine does suppress cataplexy and is sometimes used for that purpose, but switching antidepressants without recognising the underlying disorder treats one symptom while leaving the sleepiness and the diagnosis unaddressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Arrange overnight home oximetry to assess for obstructive sleep apnoea, then review
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea produces unrefreshing sleep and morning headache rather than refreshing naps, and her body mass index of 23 and absence of snoring make it improbable; oximetry alone is also a poor test in adolescents. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and a structured sleep hygiene programme
options.rationale: She has no difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep and sleeps 9 hours a night, so insomnia therapy targets a problem she does not have. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy guidance

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy typically begins in adolescence or early adult life and is frequently misattributed to depression, laziness or poor sleep habits, with reported diagnostic delays of many years. The cardinal symptom is excessive daytime sleepiness with naps that are short and refreshing, which distinguishes it from the unrefreshing sleepiness of sleep apnoea, depression and insufficient sleep. Cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, with consciousness fully preserved, is specific to narcolepsy type 1 and reflects loss of hypocretin-producing neurons in the hypothalamus. Sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations complete the classical tetrad but are neither sensitive nor specific on their own. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test, and treatment combines scheduled naps with wake-promoting agents and specific therapy for cataplexy.
key_points: Short refreshing naps distinguish narcolepsy from the unrefreshing sleepiness of apnoea or depression
Cataplexy is emotion-triggered loss of tone with preserved consciousness and is specific to narcolepsy type 1
Diagnosis requires polysomnography first, then a multiple sleep latency test the following day
Retained interest, enjoyment and reactivity argue against major depression as the explanation
Treatment combines scheduled naps, wake-promoting agents and specific anticataplectic therapy
explanation.pearls: Antidepressants suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can mask the sleep onset rapid eye movement periods that the multiple sleep latency test relies on, so they usually need to be withdrawn about 2 weeks before the study under sleep physician supervision.

subtopic_detail: Parenteral sedation for acute behavioural disturbance after novel psychoactive substance use
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 23-year-old man is brought in by police at 2 am, pacing, shouting at staff and repeatedly trying to leave through the ambulance bay. His friend says he smoked a synthetic product bought online about 2 hours ago and has had nothing else.

Verbal de-escalation in a quiet room has been attempted for 20 minutes by two experienced nurses and he has refused oral medication twice. He is now pushing past staff towards the doors and there is a genuine risk of injury to him and others.

He is sweating, his pupils measure 5 mm and react, he is moving all four limbs vigorously and there is no focal neurological deficit. A blood glucose taken at triage was 5.8 mmol/L (4.0-7.8) and a 12-lead electrocardiogram recorded earlier in the evening at another hospital showed sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 420 ms. He has no known cardiac history, no allergies and no alcohol on his breath.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, pupils 5 mm and reactive, moving all four limbs vigorously, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 5.8 mmol/L (4.0-7.8), 12-lead electrocardiogram earlier this evening in sinus rhythm with corrected QT interval 420 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly is the first line parenteral sedative in Australian emergency practice for acute behavioural disturbance, supported by randomised trials showing faster and more reliable sedation than midazolam with less respiratory depression. Its recorded corrected QT interval of 420 ms is well within the range at which droperidol at this dose has been shown to be safe. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Midazolam 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Midazolam sedates effectively but causes significantly more respiratory depression and airway intervention than droperidol at equivalent effect, which is why Australian protocols moved it to second line. It remains the agent of choice where an antipsychotic is contraindicated. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.text: Haloperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with promethazine 50 mg in the same syringe
options.rationale: This combination is used in some international settings but is not the Australian first line, and haloperidol at this dose carries a higher burden of dystonia and akathisia than droperidol without better sedation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Intramuscular olanzapine is a reasonable option but is slower in onset than droperidol and must not be combined with parenteral benzodiazepines because of cardiorespiratory depression, which limits its usefulness when escalation may be needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Ketamine 300 mg intramuscularly with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring
options.rationale: Ketamine is a rescue agent for sedation failure after two agents, and using it first exposes the patient to emergence phenomena, hypersalivation and a higher rate of intubation than necessary. (Source: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is a medical emergency in which the risk of harm to the patient and to staff has to be balanced against the risks of sedation itself. Australian practice follows a graded approach: environmental and verbal de-escalation first, then oral medication if accepted, then parenteral sedation, with physical restraint used only for the minimum time needed to give medication safely. Droperidol became the preferred parenteral agent in Australia after trials showed it achieved sedation faster than midazolam with fewer airway interventions, and concerns about QT prolongation at the doses used in this setting were not borne out. Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists and other novel psychoactive substances are not detected on routine urine drug screens, produce far more severe agitation, tachycardia and hyperthermia than plant cannabis, and are recognised causes of seizures and acute kidney injury. After sedation, the priorities are continuous monitoring, a temperature check for hyperthermia, creatine kinase for rhabdomyolysis, and reassessment for an organic cause.
key_points: De-escalate and offer oral medication before parenteral sedation, and restrain only for the minimum time needed
Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly is the Australian first line parenteral agent, with midazolam second line
Ketamine is a rescue agent after failure of two sedatives, not a first choice
Synthetic cannabinoids are not detected on routine urine drug screens and cause more severe toxicity than plant cannabis
After sedation check temperature, creatine kinase and glucose, and reassess for a medical cause of the disturbance
explanation.pearls: Hyperthermia above 38.5 °C in a stimulant or synthetic cannabinoid presentation demands active cooling and a creatine kinase level, because it is the single best predictor of rhabdomyolysis and death in this group.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

subtopic_detail: Assessing new behaviour change in a minimally verbal adult before altering psychotropic medication
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a disability mental health service. A 28-year-old man with severe intellectual disability who uses about six signs and no spoken words is reviewed at the request of his group home.

For 6 weeks he has been striking the right side of his own face with an open hand, has refused about half his meals and has begun waking and calling out around 3 am. Staff report no change of housemates, keyworker or daily routine over the past 6 months, and no change in his day programme.

He has taken risperidone 1 mg daily for 4 years. The house manager has asked you to increase it. His bowel chart shows a soft formed stool every day for the past fortnight and he passed urine normally at the start of the consultation.

On examination he is reluctant to open his mouth and grimaces and pulls away when you touch his right cheek, though he tolerates palpation of the left. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. His temperature and other observations are normal and there is no rash or swelling visible over the jaw.

data_table.Examination: Reluctant to open mouth, grimaces and withdraws on palpation of the right cheek but tolerates the left, soft non-tender abdomen, no visible facial swelling or rash
data_table.Observations: Bowel chart with a soft formed stool daily for the past fortnight, normal urine output observed
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 1 mg daily for 4 years, no recent changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase risperidone to 2 mg daily and ask staff to record the behaviour for 4 weeks
options.rationale: Increasing an antipsychotic in response to behaviour change without first excluding a physical cause is the anti-pattern known as diagnostic overshadowing, and it adds metabolic and extrapyramidal risk while leaving the source of pain untreated. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Start citalopram for a presumed depressive episode and review his sleep in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Depression can indeed present as behaviour change and sleep disturbance in intellectual disability, but it is a diagnosis reached after physical causes are excluded, and nothing here explains the strictly unilateral facial signs. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Arrange a dental examination under sedation to assess the localised facial findings
options.rationale: New self-injury directed repeatedly at one body site, with food refusal, night waking and unilateral tenderness on that side, points to localised pain, and dental disease is the commonest treatable cause in adults with severe intellectual disability who cannot report toothache. Examination under sedation is often the only way to obtain an adequate look and to treat in the same episode. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Request an abdominal radiograph to assess for faecal loading as a cause of his distress
options.rationale: Constipation is a leading cause of behaviour change in this population and is always worth considering, but his bowel chart documents a soft formed stool daily and his abdomen is soft and non-tender, which makes it an unlikely explanation here. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

options.text: Commission a functional behaviour assessment with a positive behaviour support plan
options.rationale: Functional behaviour assessment is a core part of management for established behaviours of concern, but it starts from the premise that the behaviour is environmentally maintained, and here the history of abrupt onset with no environmental change and localised physical signs points elsewhere first. (Source: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability)
source_refs: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

explanation.summary: Adults with severe intellectual disability who have little or no speech communicate physical distress through behaviour, and a new or escalating behaviour of concern should be treated as a symptom needing a differential diagnosis rather than as a reason to increase psychotropic medication. Diagnostic overshadowing, the attribution of new symptoms to the intellectual disability or to a known psychiatric diagnosis, is the central error to avoid. The physical causes worth systematically excluding are dental disease, constipation, gastro-oesophageal reflux, urinary retention or infection, otitis media, fracture, menstrual pain and medication adverse effects including akathisia. Useful discriminators are the abruptness of onset, whether anything in the environment changed, whether the behaviour targets a particular body region, and whether sleep and appetite changed at the same time. Psychotropic reduction rather than escalation is the direction of travel in Australian policy, given the long history of overprescribing in this population.
key_points: New behaviour change in a minimally verbal adult is a symptom requiring a differential diagnosis, not an automatic dose increase
Diagnostic overshadowing is the error of attributing new symptoms to the disability or existing diagnosis
Exclude dental disease, constipation, reflux, urinary and ear infection, fracture and akathisia
Behaviour targeting one body site with unilateral tenderness points to localised pain
Australian policy direction is psychotropic reduction with positive behaviour support, not escalation
explanation.pearls: Akathisia from an existing antipsychotic can itself present as agitation and self-injury, so a dose increase can worsen the very behaviour it is meant to treat; ask staff specifically whether the person can now sit still for a meal or a television programme.

sources.label: RANZCP: Position statement on the mental health of people with intellectual disability

subtopic_detail: Selecting a relapse prevention strategy when adherence and substance use have both been excluded
stem:
You are the registrar in an early psychosis service. A 22-year-old man is admitted with his second relapse in 10 months, 18 months after a first episode of schizophrenia.

He has received paliperidone palmitate depot on the due date every month, documented on the depot register, and a trough plasma level taken on admission sits in the expected therapeutic range. A urine drug screen on admission is negative for cannabis, amphetamines and other substances, as it was at his previous admission.

He lives with both parents. During family sessions his mother interrupts and speaks for him for much of the hour, and his father describes him as lazy and says he should be looking for work. The nursing notes record that both relapses were preceded by several days of escalating arguments at home about his daily routine. On the ward his symptoms settle within 10 days without a dose change. He can describe his early warning signs, accepts he has an illness and wants to stay well. The consultant asks you what to prioritise for discharge planning.

data_table.Mental state: Settled by day 10 without a dose change, accepts the illness, able to name his own early warning signs
data_table.Investigations: Paliperidone trough plasma level within the expected therapeutic range, urine drug screen negative at this and the previous admission
data_table.Collateral: Depot register shows every dose given on the due date; both relapses preceded by days of escalating conflict at home

lead_in: What is most likely to reduce his risk of a further relapse?

options.text: Increase the paliperidone palmitate depot to the next dose band before discharge
options.rationale: A therapeutic plasma level with symptom resolution in 10 days without any dose change argues that the dose was not the limiting factor, and escalating it adds extrapyramidal and prolactin burden without addressing what preceded both relapses. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Arrange behavioural family intervention with psychoeducation for the whole household
options.rationale: Behavioural family intervention is the intervention with the strongest evidence for relapse reduction in schizophrenia, roughly halving relapse rates over the following 2 years when delivered over at least 10 sessions, and it is specifically indicated where criticism and over-involvement are prominent at home. With adherence confirmed by the depot register and plasma level and substance use excluded twice, the family environment is the modifiable factor that both relapses point to. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Add sodium valproate as an augmenting agent and review his mental state in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Anticonvulsant augmentation has little evidence in schizophrenia without a mood component or aggression, and it adds hepatic, haematological and teratogenic monitoring burden for no expected relapse benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Switch him to clozapine, with the mandatory haematological monitoring protocol started
options.rationale: Clozapine is indicated after failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials, whereas his symptoms remitted on his current agent both times, so this is relapse in a responsive illness rather than treatment resistance. The distinguishing question is whether the drug failed to control symptoms or whether something outside the drug precipitated relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Provide weekly individual supportive counselling with the case manager after discharge
options.rationale: Individual supportive contact maintains engagement and is valuable, but it has not been shown to reduce relapse in the way structured family intervention has, and it leaves the household dynamic that preceded both relapses unaddressed. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

explanation.summary: When a person with schizophrenia relapses, the reflex explanations are non-adherence and substance use, and these account for the majority of cases, which is why a long-acting injectable register and a urine drug screen are checked first. Once both are excluded and plasma levels confirm adequate exposure, the differential moves to psychosocial precipitants, and the best studied of these is the emotional climate of the household. Research on expressed emotion has consistently shown that high levels of criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement in relatives predict relapse, and that structured family intervention reduces it. Effective programmes run for at least 10 sessions over 6 months or more and combine psychoeducation, communication training and structured problem solving with the whole family rather than the patient alone. Family intervention is recommended in Australian and international guidelines yet remains substantially underdelivered, in part because services default to individual work.
key_points: Exclude non-adherence and substance use first, using the depot register, plasma levels and urine screening
High expressed emotion at home, meaning criticism, hostility or over-involvement, predicts relapse
Behavioural family intervention of at least 10 sessions roughly halves relapse rates
Clozapine is for treatment resistance after two adequate trials, not for relapse in a drug-responsive illness
A therapeutic plasma level with rapid remission argues against the dose being the problem
explanation.pearls: Family intervention needs a minimum of 10 sessions over 6 months to show relapse benefit; single-session psychoeducation for relatives improves knowledge but has not been shown to change relapse rates.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders
